newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Bhutto's husband seen as her Achilles' heel.
newsitem.headline: Bhutto's husband seen as her Achilles' heel.

text.p: Asif Ali Zardari, detained since his wife Benazir Bhutto was unceremoniously sacked as prime minister, is widely seen as her greatest liability.
The smooth businessman, one month younger than Bhutto at 43, is once again embroiled in allegations that he was at the centre of a web of sleaze that tainted the ousted government.
In 1994 Zardari was cleared of the last of 13 similar charges brought against him after the first Bhutto government was dismissed by presidential order four years earlier.

This time soldiers seized Zardari at the governor's house in the Punjab provincial capital Lahore, where he had been staying, in the early hours of Tuesday, shortly after President Farooq Leghari abruptly ended Bhutto's three-year rule.
Transferred to a resthouse near Islamabad, he was kept incommunicado for 48 hours before a furious Bhutto and their three children were permitted to visit him late at night.
Bhutto had threatened to bring a kidnapping charge against Leghari unless her lawyer was given access to her husband.
The caretaker government led by Prime Minister Meraj Khalid first said Zardari was being held in protective custody and then cited maintenance of public order to justify his detention.

Few doubt that serious charges will be brought against Zardari, the main focus of corruption allegations swirling around the former government, in which he served as investment minister for its last turbulent four months.
More ominously, his name has been linked to the killing of Bhutto's estranged brother Murtaza Bhutto by police in Karachi.

Lawyers for Murtaza's widow Ghinwa have said Zardari was involved in a conspiracy with former interior minister Naseerullah Babar and former Sindh province chief minister Abdullah Shah that led to Murtaza's death on September 20.
Zardari has denied all the allegations against him and continues to enjoy unstinted public support from his wife.
"I think they are waiting to fabricate some charges against him," she told Reuters on Thursday. "Obviously there are no charges against him, so they need the time."
She said she suspected that pressure would be brought on Ghinwa to file murder charges against her husband.
Throughout her government Bhutto defended Zardari against charges of abusing his position for personal gain, just as she did during her 30 months in power from 1988 to 1990.
Then too he denied any wrongdoing, but became a target of corruption inquiries after the 1990 dismissal and was arrested in connection with extortion and illegal bank loan cases.
Courts cleared him of the charges as well as one of conspiring to murder 29 people who died when gunmen fired on activists of Karachi's Mohajir National Movement in 1990.
Now, as then, it may be hard to make charges stick against Zardari, but his reputation among his countrymen could remain besmirched by pervasive talk of his wheeling and dealing.
The news that Pakistan's most famous political leader was to wed Zardari took Pakistan by surprise in July 1987.

As the product of a traditional Sindhi land-owning family, like the Bhuttos, he was charming and eligible enough. But as an avid polo player who liked to frequent discos and nightclubs, he seemed an odd match for the dedicated political activist.
Zardari made a brief and unsuccessful foray into politics in 1985, before withdrawing to concentrate on running his father's estates and family business until the 1990 polls.
His father Hakim Ali Zardari, an associate of Bhutto's father Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, was elected to parliament for his Pakistan People's Party in 1970 but left the party in 1976.
His mother is a friend of Bhutto's mother, Nusrat, who is said to have played a major role in setting up the match.
Zardari tried to keep a low profile after the marriage, claiming he would leave politics to his wife.
But he won a National Assembly seat in 1990 from Karachi's slum area of Lyari while in jail, and served as water and power minister in a caretaker government formed in April 1993.

Born in Nawabshah in southern Pakistan on July 26, 1953, he was educated in Karachi and Petaro near Hyderabad. He later studied at St Patrick College in Karachi and took an economics diploma from a London college.
He is a passionate polo player and likes squash and tennis. He is also found of clay-pigeon shooting.
He and Bhutto have a son, Bilawal, and two daughters, Bakhtawar and Asifa.
